we have had no evidence to the contrary- and that it is carrying out the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act.

Coming down to the seaboard, under the same item, 433, "the provisions of the conventions for the safety of life at sea and load-lines," what action is the government going to take, in view of the present emergency in foreign affairs, on the ocean if there is any trouble during the coming year?-and from what the Prime Minister and others have said in this chamber, we may be pretty close to it. What action is the government taking in view of the fact that we have now only 120 convoy ships to transport all this food and man-power and look after our trade on the seven seas? We have less than before the war. What action is the government taking to look after the civilian population in connection with the transport of food, and for the safety of passengers and crews and the merchant marine at sea? Seeing that there are 2,000 ships less in the British merchant marine, including Canadian hulls, than before the war, the government must be taking some precautions for the safety not only of ocean liners but of ships of the merchant marine which convey food and supplies to the mother country. The government sends representatives to the convention which is held during the imperial conference; there was a shipping committee, and Canada is on that committee. In what way is this item related to what is done, or is not done-because Canada refused to do anything about shipping at the convention, although she sends representatives from the department to the conferences. We should get some report from them. What is the policy of Canada, in view of the emergency, as regards safety at sea?

I may say that all the international life-saving conventions have been complied with. We have adopted every international convention having to do with the safety of shipping at sea, and as I stated before, our inspection staffs are carrying out as efficiently as possible the terms of the Canada Shipping Act- and the various conventions.
They are not doing anything. The minister might just as well say, no.
I may say to my hon. friend that in the last two years we have doubled the size of the Canadian navy.
Not a thing has been done.
How is the charge for the inspection of these ships made up? On what basis is it computed? Are all the boats in Canada, including those on the lakes, subject to these inspections?

All passenger boats and all cargo boats above 150 tons. Under 500 tons the cost of the load line certificate is S30; the renewal certificate, $10, and the annual survey, $10. From 500 tons to 1,000 tons, the cost of the certificate is $40; from 1,000 tons to 2,000 tons, $55; 2,000 tons, $65; 3,000 tons, $70; 4,000 tons, $75; and up to 9,000 and over, $100.
Is that for each inspection?

That is for the issue of the certificate. For the renewal of the certificate the . cost is $25, and the annual survey is $20.
Mr. MaeINNIS: What is the amount collected under this?
About $120,000 per annum altogether.
Last year it was
Yes.

What is the operating loss? The estimate last year was $200,000, and we collected $112,000. Is there any reason why the dominion government should stand
that loss?

Our inspectors do a great
deal of work for which there is no charge. Apart from the annual inspection fee, the inspector goes aboard frequently to make interim inspections for which no charge is made. Replying to my hon. friend's question, I think we would be justified in increasing the fees in order to make the steamship inspection branch self-supporting. I shall be glad to have our officers look into the situation and make recommendations.

I am glad to hear the minister say that. It seems to me that the value of this service to shipping is so very important from the point of view of insurance rates, safety and the hazards encountered, that the department should make it self-supporting or make a profit out of it if necessary.

The boats that ply out of Toronto harbour, the Kingston and the Toronto, are forty or fifty years old, and while they look seaworthy I think they should be inspected, seeing that they are so old. I suggest that all these passenger boats on the great lakes should be equipped with the latest type of radio. That is important.

Supply-Transport-Marine Service

The law requires all passenger boats to carry radio and those of more than 5,000 tons to carry radio in the fall of the year, and in addition to that we are providing telephone service. We have expanded that a great deal within the last year. We have radio and telephone services at a number of points along the shore on the great lakes, and a great number of very small boats are installing telephones. This allows the shore stations to communicate with the boat and vice versa. The boat can connect with the Bell system so that the master may talk with head office or with his wife at home. This service is attracting a good deal of attention, and we are ahead of the United States in this regard. The United States, however, have this year made a considerable appropriation for a similar service on that side. I rather think that by next year we shall be able to make the use of either the telephone or the radiotelegraph mandatory for all shipping of any size on the lakes.

There is another matter that should be attended to. The lifeboats on these steamers are forty or fifty years old. The boats are pretty well worn out, having been painted and repainted, the paint having been burnt off frequently. Is there a rigid inspection of these life-boats, or is there a time limit for their replacement?

There is an annual inspection of life-boats. The regidations are similar to those of the British Board of Trade, and they are rigid. I can assure my hon. friend that the life-boats are in first-class condition. I cannot believe that the life-boats on these steamers are of any great age.
Are there no regulations governing vessels under 150 tons? Are they not inspected?

All passenger boats, however small, are inspected, but cargo boats up to 15 tons are exempt. The cost of inspecting these small boats adds considerably to the cost of the inspection service. We found it desirable to charge a small fee. It costs a good deal to inspect a small boat, and the real loss by the department is on account of the fact that the fee charged for the inspection of small boats is inadequate. But the desirability of the service from the point of view of safety of life warrants our doing the work at a small fee.
The number of tackle inspectors has been doubled this year. Do these inspectors look over the tackle used by longshoremen in loading and unloading?

These men inspect all kinds of tackle and examine especially the chains for flaws. They also inspect methods of loading. We have doubled the number of inspectors because we thought there were too many accidents where ports did not have tackle inspectors.

The minister said that he would take into consideration a proposal to increase some of the tariffs charged for inspection services. Personally I am not very much in favour of any increase for inspection services unless it is absolutely imperative. Last year we passed certain legislation which put a good many carriers under considerable handicap. Personally I was in favour of that legislation, but I hardly think it would be an appropriate time to place further handicaps by way of increased tariff tolls on the people engaged in that traffic. It is a service for which the government have a responsibility, the same as many other inspection services which the government owe to the public for its protection. The government ought to bear part of the responsibility, and cannot make the service entirely self-supporting. There are many other services given by the government, such as inspection of weights and measures, for which we do not charge. It is done for the protection of the public, and the same applies in a sense in regard to the load-line and so on. I feel that we should not make the cost too onerous, particularly for the smaller boats.
My hon. friend is incorrect when he says there is no charge for inspection in connection with weights and measures. There is a charge made.
But does it carry itself?
It does.

Then my argument in that respect is not sound, but there are other phases of government inspection in which service is given practically free of charge because in some measure it is for the protection of the public.

I moved for a return to an order of the house in this connection, and I have not received the return. The order relates to conventions for safety at sea, and the load-line. I have asked for that return four or five times.
In connection with this item I wish to ask two or three questions. There are United States ships now carrying Canadian grain; in view of the amendments to the Canada-United States trade treaty, have we any control over those ships or load-lines? What inspection is there?



Supply-Mines and Resources
The minister's department has in the last few years sold for $50,000 a number of ships costing $1,000,000, $1,500,000, $1,750,000, $2,000,000. Did he look into the load-line there; were they inspected before the sale, and did lie consider that in an emergency we may need those very ships to carry food and supplies to the old country? They could have been converted into merchant ships. Why were they sold? The admiralty has announced that they are 2,000 ships short at the present time.
Another question was regarding representations which were made by marine bodies, navigators, the engineers' and mates' association and others regarding aids to navigation and the safety of crews on the great lakes. Under the British North America Act there has to be equality of treatment for ships on the great lakes or the St. Lawrence or the ocean regarding registry and aids to navigation. Surely men on ships on the great lakes are entitled to some inspection and regulation of load-line.
The minister said that they have doubled Canada's navy, I asked for a return on that too as correlated to this item. What is the fleet?
If I may interrupt, let me say that since my hon. friend has not obtained his return, this item may stand and I shall see that the return is brought down immediately.
My remarks were on the minister's own statement three or four minutes ago. I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The item stands.
I had not finished what I had to say about the load-line. I have something yet to say about this item. I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is out of order. The item stands.
The rest of what I have to say will be relevant to this very item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member must resume his seat.
The item stands whenever anyone wants to say anything.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order.
Item stands.
mines and resources
118. Departmental administration, $178,735.

The estimates of this
department are now being considered for the first time?
Quite.
How many other departments are there whose estimates have not yet been considered for the first time?
I cannot say at the moment. I do not think there are many.

I do not wish to delay the proceedings, but this is the one occasion, when the government does choose to move to go into supply, when hon. members might possibly bring up some subject for redress. I will not object to the estimates of this department being introduced at the present time, but I do not think it should be done too often in this way at the last moment.
It has not been done very frequently, I think.

As a matter of fact, never has.there been a government that I know of while I have been in this house which has moved so seldom to go into supply as this government. This government has done so as rarely as possible, apparently for the purpose of dodging the possibility of some private member bringing up a controversial subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend said supply was not important.

I have explained that. I said estimates were only fillers in, and that is correct; but I do not want them filled in quite so easily all the time, because there may be an occasion when we wish to take up some subject. However, I do not wish to delay the introduction of the estimates of this department getting in. I have nothing in view in regard to moving an amendment, but I hope that one of these days the government will move to go into supply and give us an opportunity if we wish to bring up anything.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, the item will not carry. We will discuss that next time.
Item stands.

Apparently the Postmaster-general is getting ready with his estimates. I do not want it understood that the estimates of the Post Office Department have been brought in for the first time without a little discussion. We have allowed one department in; I do not like to hold up the new minister, but at the same time I do not think he should count himself in at the present time.

I think under those circumstances we can meet the wishes of the leader of the opposition. He has really cooperated pretty well, especially during the last week or so.

Questions

We have been cooperating all the time.
Progress reported.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
